# Nevada Contract, Warranty and Consumer-Protection Law

Research file for the Las Vegas new construction buyer guide.

- **Researched:** 2026-07-25
- **Geography:** Clark County, Nevada. Nevada state law applies statewide, so the statutes below are not Clark County specific, but every practical example is framed for Las Vegas, North Las Vegas, Henderson, Summerlin, Spring Valley, Enterprise, Paradise, Centennial Hills, Skye Canyon, Mountain's Edge, Inspirada, Cadence, Union Village and Sunrise Manor.
- **Currency of the statutes:** Every NRS chapter cited here was pulled from the Nevada Legislature site on 2026-07-25 and each page carries the header "[Rev. 4/15/2026 ... --2025]", meaning the text reflects law through the 2025 legislative session. Chapter revision stamps confirmed: NRS 11, NRS 40, NRS 113, NRS 116, NRS 597, NRS 624, NRS 645, NRS 645D.
- **Framing:** This is plain-language buyer education, not legal advice. The finished guide must carry a line telling readers to consult a Nevada attorney for their own situation.

---

## 1. NRS Chapter 40: Nevada's constructional defect law

### 1.1 What it covers

"Constructional defect" means a defect in the design, construction, manufacture, repair or landscaping of a new residence, of an alteration of or addition to an existing residence, or of an appurtenance, which either (1) presents an unreasonable risk of injury to a person or property, or (2) is not completed in a good and workmanlike manner and proximately causes physical damage to the residence, an appurtenance or the real property to which it is affixed [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.615).

NRS 40.600 to 40.695 apply to any constructional defect claim except a claim for personal injury or wrongful death, they prevail over any conflicting law, they do not bar defenses otherwise available, and they do not create a new theory of liability [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.635).

**Plain-language point for the guide:** the two-part test matters. A cosmetic complaint that does not create a safety risk and does not cause physical damage may not qualify as a "constructional defect" under Chapter 40, even if the homeowner is unhappy with it. Those items belong in the punch list and the warranty process instead.

### 1.2 The claim process, step by step, with the actual deadlines

**Step 1. Written notice to the builder.** Before a homeowner can file suit or add a defect cause of action, the homeowner must give written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the contractor at the address in the State Contractors Board records, the county or city clerk records, or the contractor's last known address. The notice must (a) state it is being given to satisfy this section, (b) specify in reasonable detail the defects, damages or injuries for each residence, (c) describe in reasonable detail the cause if known and the nature and extent of resulting damage, and (d) include a signed verification statement from each named owner. A homeowners association representative may send the notice on the association's behalf, signed under penalty of perjury by a board member or officer [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.645).

Notice is not required first if the contractor has already sued the homeowner, or if the homeowner has filed a formal complaint with law enforcement against the contractor for threatening or committing violence or a criminal offense (NRS 40.645(4)).

**Step 2. Let them in to look.** After notice, the homeowner must give the contractor and any responsible subcontractor, supplier or design professional reasonable access to the home to determine the nature and extent of the defect and of any repairs needed. Those inspecting must coordinate to minimize inconvenience to the homeowner [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.6462).

**Step 3. Be present, point it out, allow repair.** Before suing, the homeowner must allow the inspection, be present or have a representative present and reasonably identify where the defects are, and allow a reasonable opportunity to repair if the builder elects to repair. If a homeowner sues without doing this, the court must either dismiss without prejudice and compel compliance, or stay the case if dismissal would let the limitation or repose period run out [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.647).

**Step 4. The builder's written response: 90 days.** A written response must be sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, by the contractor not later than **90 days** after the contractor receives the notice, and by any noticed subcontractor, supplier or design professional not later than **90 days** after they receive it. The response must address each defect and must state whether the responder elects to repair or to have the defect repaired. If the repair will force the homeowner out of the home, the election must also include money reasonably necessary for temporary housing, storage of household items, or both. The response may include a proposal for money compensation and may disclaim liability with reasons [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.6472).

If the claimant is a homeowners association, the association must send a copy of the response to every member within **30 days** of receiving it (NRS 40.6472(3)). If the builder elects **not** to repair, the homeowner may bring the claim (NRS 40.6472(4)). If the builder elects **to** repair, the homeowner must give a reasonable opportunity to repair (NRS 40.6472(5)).

**Step 5. If the builder elects to repair: 105 or 150 days.** Unless the parties agree to extend, repairs must be completed **not later than 105 days** after the notice was received when the notice came from four or fewer owners, or **not later than 150 days** when it came from five or more owners or from a homeowners association representative. If repairs reasonably cannot be finished in that window, the parties must agree on a reasonable time, and if they cannot agree, any of them may petition the court to set one [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.648(2) and (3)).

Repairs must be done on reasonable dates and times agreed in advance, in compliance with the applicable building code, in a good and workmanlike manner to the generally accepted standard of care for that repair, and in a way that does not raise the cost of maintaining the home unless the builder agrees in writing to cover the increase. Non-defective parts of the home that must be removed to fix the defect must be replaced. The builder must prevent, remove and indemnify against mechanics and materialmens liens (NRS 40.648(1)).

**An election to repair may not be made conditional upon a release of liability** [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.648(4)). This is a strong buyer-protective point worth stating plainly in the guide: a Nevada builder cannot lawfully condition a Chapter 40 repair on the homeowner signing away their rights.

**Step 6. Written repair statement: 30 days after repairs.** Not later than **30 days** after repairs are completed, the party who made or caused the repairs must give the homeowner a written statement describing the nature and extent of the repair, the method used, and the extent of any materials or parts replaced [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.648(5)).

**Step 7. Mediation before suit.** Before filing, the matter must go to mediation unless both sides waive it in writing. The parties pick a mediator by agreement, and if they cannot agree within **20 days** after the claimant first selects one, any party may petition the American Arbitration Association, the Nevada Arbitration Association, Nevada Dispute Resolution Services or another acceptable service to appoint one. The mediator must convene the mediation within **30 days** and complete it within **45 days** after the matter is submitted, unless extended by agreement. The claimant deposits **$50** with the mediation service and the other parties split the rest of the estimated fees. Unless otherwise agreed, total fees for each day of mediation and the mediator must not exceed **$750 per day** [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.680).

Premediation discovery is due not later than **15 days** before mediation begins (NRS 40.681).

### 1.3 The special fast track for brand new homes: NRS 40.672

This one deserves its own callout in the guide. If a contractor, subcontractor, supplier or design professional receives written notice of a constructional defect **not more than 1 year after the close of escrow of the initial purchase of the residence**, they must make the repairs **within 45 days** after receiving the written notice, unless delayed by the claimant or by events beyond their control, or unless timely completion is not reasonably possible. The parties may agree in writing to extend. A contractor or subcontractor who fails to comply is immediately subject to discipline under NRS 624.300 [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.672).

**Why this matters to a buyer:** in the first year after closing, Nevada law puts the builder on a much shorter clock (45 days) than the general Chapter 40 process (90-day response plus 105 or 150 days to repair). It is a concrete legal reason to document problems in writing during year one rather than waiting.

### 1.4 Imminent threats to health or safety

If the defect creates an imminent threat to the health or safety of the people living in the home, the builder must take reasonable steps to cure it as soon as practicable, and may not use unlicensed people to do the work. If the builder fails to cure in a reasonable time, the owner may have it fixed and recover the reasonable cost of repairs plus reasonable attorney's fees and costs, in addition to other damages available under other law. A builder who declines to cure after a good faith reasonable inspection concluding there is no imminent threat is not liable for those fees and costs, unless a building inspector or building official with jurisdiction certifies that there is an imminent threat [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.670).

### 1.5 What a homeowner can recover

Damages are limited to: reasonable cost of necessary repairs already made and yet to be made that the contractor failed to cure, plus reasonable temporary housing during repair; reduction in market value to the extent it is because of structural failure; loss of use; reasonable value of other property damaged; additional costs reasonably incurred including expert fees to determine the nature and extent of defects, evaluate corrective measures and estimate loss of use, temporary housing cost and market value reduction; and any interest provided by statute. If a contractor complies with NRS 40.600 to 40.695, the claimant may not recover any other damages from that contractor for the defect. "Structural failure" means physical damage to the load-bearing portion of the residence caused by a failure of that load-bearing portion [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.655).

**Note the gap:** reduction in market value is recoverable only "to the extent the reduction is because of structural failure" (NRS 40.655(1)(b)). A non-structural defect that hurts resale value does not automatically produce a market-value damage award.

### 1.6 Penalties for playing games, on both sides

If a homeowner unreasonably rejects a reasonable written settlement offer made in the builder's response and then sues, the court may deny the homeowner's attorney's fees and costs and may award fees and costs to the contractor. Any sums paid under a builder's warranty, other than sums paid on claims collateral to coverage issued to or by the contractor, must be deducted from any recovery [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.650(1)).

Cutting the other way: if the builder fails to comply with NRS 40.6472, fails to make a settlement offer, fails to make a good faith response asserting no liability, refuses to agree to or accept a mediator, or refuses to participate in mediation, then the damage limits and defenses in NRS 40.600 to 40.695 **do not apply**, and the homeowner may sue without satisfying any other Chapter 40 requirement (NRS 40.650(2)).

**Homeowners must work the warranty.** "If a residence or appurtenance that is the subject of the claim is covered by a builder's warranty, a claimant shall diligently pursue a claim under the builder's warranty" [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.650(3)). This is the statutory hook that ties Chapter 40 to the 1-2-10 warranty discussion in Section 3.

### 1.7 If you later sell a home that had a Chapter 40 claim

A claimant who tries to sell a home that is or was the subject of a Chapter 40 claim must disclose in writing to any prospective purchaser, not less than **30 days** before close of escrow (or immediately on execution of the sales agreement if escrow closes in under 30 days, or within **24 hours** after giving the builder notice if the claim starts less than 30 days before closing): all notices given to the contractor, all expert opinions obtained about the defect, the terms of any settlement, order or judgment, and a detailed report of all repairs made [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.688).

### 1.8 The statute of repose: 10 years, not 6

This is the most commonly mis-stated fact in Nevada new construction content, so state it carefully.

**Current law.** No action may be commenced against the owner, occupier, or any person performing or furnishing the design, planning, supervision or observation of construction, or the construction of an improvement to real property, **more than 10 years after the substantial completion** of that improvement, for damages from (a) any deficiency in design, planning, supervision or observation of construction or the construction itself, (b) injury to real or personal property caused by such a deficiency, or (c) injury to or wrongful death of a person caused by such a deficiency [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-011.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 11.202(1)).

An action for **fraud** in causing such a deficiency may be commenced at any time after substantial completion, except that this does not apply to a lower-tiered subcontractor who covers up another trade's defect without knowing and without reason to know of it (NRS 11.202(2)). The section does not apply to claims for indemnity or contribution, to innkeeper liability claims, or to product defect claims (NRS 11.202(3)).

**When the clock starts.** The date of substantial completion is deemed to be the date on which the final building inspection is conducted, a notice of completion is issued, or a certificate of occupancy is issued, **whichever occurs later**. If none of those happens, the date is determined by common law [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-011.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 11.2055).

**Legislative history, stated accurately:**

| Period | Repose period | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Before 2015 | 6 to 10 years depending on defect type: 6 years patent, 8 years latent, 10 years known, no repose for fraud | Prior law [source: https://lewisbrisbois.com/newsroom/articles/nevada-overhauls-construction-defect-laws-for-residential-construction \| verified: 2026-07-25] |
| Feb 24, 2015 (AB 125) | Single **6-year** repose for all defects, from substantial completion | AB 125, signed Feb 24, 2015 [source: https://nevadabuilders.org/summary-of-ab-125/ \| verified: 2026-07-25] |
| Oct 1, 2019 (AB 421) | Raised back to **10 years** | AB 421, signed June 3, 2019, effective Oct 1, 2019 [source: https://www.wshblaw.com/nevadas-governor-signs-chapter-40-reform-bill/ \| verified: 2026-07-25] |

The 2015 and 2019 amendments are both reflected in the statute's own history note, which reads "(Added to NRS by 1983, 1238; A 2015, 17; 2019, 2262)" [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-011.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Retroactivity:** secondary sources report that the 2019 change applies retroactively to improvements substantially completed before October 1, 2019, and that the Nevada Supreme Court has addressed the retroactive nature of the 10-year repose [source: https://www.grsm.com/insight/nevada-supreme-court-clarifies-retroactive-nature-of-10-year-statute-of-repose-for-construction-and-design-defects/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. **Do not put the retroactivity holding in reader-facing prose.** It is a litigation question and adds nothing for a buyer. Exact case name and citation: NOT FOUND (not independently verified in this pass).

### 1.9 Tolling

Statutes of limitation or repose on a Chapter 40 defect claim are tolled from the time notice of the claim is given until the earlier of (a) **one year** after notice is given, or (b) **30 days** after mediation is concluded or waived in writing. Tolling longer than one year requires the claimant to show the court good cause. Tolling applies to third parties whether or not they must appear [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 40.695).

### 1.10 What AB 125 (2015) changed

AB 125, signed February 24, 2015 and titled the "Homeowner Protections Act of 2015," substantially rewrote NRS 40.600 et seq. Reported changes [source: https://nevadabuilders.org/summary-of-ab-125/ | verified: 2026-07-25] and [source: https://lewisbrisbois.com/newsroom/articles/nevada-overhauls-construction-defect-laws-for-residential-construction | verified: 2026-07-25]:

1. **Narrowed the definition** of constructional defect to the two-part test now in NRS 40.615, and removed building code violations and industry standards as standalone bases for a claim.
2. **Removed the near-automatic recovery of attorney's fees** by claimants.
3. **Collapsed the repose periods into a single 6-year period** (since raised to 10 years by AB 421 in 2019).
4. **Tightened notice content**, requiring defects, damages and injuries to be specified in reasonable detail per residence with signed owner verification (now NRS 40.645(2)).
5. **Required the claimant or the claimant's expert to be present at the inspection** and to identify the proximate locations of the defects (now NRS 40.647(1)(b)).
6. **Restricted homeowners association standing** to sue representatively for individual unit owners, limiting them largely to common elements. Association standing was partially restored in 2019.
7. **Required homeowners to pursue an available builder's warranty.** AB 421 (2019) softened this: a claimant need only "diligently pursue" the warranty claim, and it is no longer a precondition to serving a Chapter 40 notice [source: https://www.wshblaw.com/nevadas-governor-signs-chapter-40-reform-bill/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

The individual section history notes on leg.state.nv.us independently confirm 2015 amendments to NRS 40.615, 40.635, 40.645, 40.6462, 40.647, 40.6472, 40.648, 40.650, 40.655 and 40.695 [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Exact AB 125 and AB 421 bill-page URLs on leg.state.nv.us:** NOT FOUND (the statutory text and its history notes were verified directly, but the NELIS bill overview URLs were not retrieved in this pass).

## 2. NRS 624.600 to 624.630: what a residential builder must disclose and provide

### 2.1 NRS 624.602, the statutory builder's warranty (the single most useful section for this guide)

A licensee who completes construction of a new, single-family residence **shall provide to the purchaser**:

- **(a)** a separate, single-page disclosure describing the purchaser's rights under NRS Chapter 624, including the right to file a complaint under NRS 624.480 seeking recovery from the Residential Recovery Fund established under NRS 624.470; and
- **(b)** a builder's warranty that meets the requirements of the section.

The builder's warranty must:

- **Be in writing.**
- **Be valid for a period of at least 1 year from the date of completion of a written punch list.** "Punch list" means a list of any materials or work describing incomplete or incorrect installations or incidental damage to existing finishes, material and structures that do not conform to the contract specifications or to NRS 624.3017(1).
- **Contain terms warrantying, without limitation, all home systems, workmanship, materials, plumbing, electrical and mechanical systems, appliances installed by contractors, fixtures, equipment and structural components**, unless a separate warranty is provided by the manufacturer or installer of that product, component or system.
- **Be transferable to a subsequent purchaser** of the residence.
- **Not be construed as a waiver or release of any other warranty** from the licensee provided by contract or otherwise available under Nevada law.

[source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-624.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 624.602). Added to NRS by 2019 (AB 421).

**Three buyer-facing takeaways:**
1. Nevada law requires a written builder warranty of **at least one year** on a new single-family home, and the clock runs from completion of the **written punch list**, not from closing. If there is no written punch list, the start date is unclear, which is a reason to insist on a written punch list at the blue tape walkthrough.
2. The warranty is **transferable**. A buyer purchasing a nearly-new home from its first owner should ask for the warranty documents.
3. The warranty **cannot be used to waive** other warranties the builder gave by contract or that Nevada law provides.

### 2.2 NRS 624.600, subcontractor and lien disclosures

A general building contractor shall provide in writing to the owner of a single-family residence with whom it has contracted: (a) the name, license number, business address and telephone number of all subcontractors it has contracted with on the project and all persons furnishing material valued at **$500 or more**; (b) notice that such a person may record a notice of lien on the residence under NRS 108.226; and (c) an informational form prescribed by the State Contractors Board about contractors under Chapter 624 and about mechanics and materialmens liens under Chapter 108 [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-624.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 624.600).

**Caveat for accuracy:** NRS 624.600 by its terms applies to a general building contractor and "the owner of a single-family residence ... with whom he or she has contracted." That language fits a custom build or a remodel where the homeowner contracts directly with the builder. In a production-builder tract sale the builder owns the lot and sells a finished home, so the subcontractor-list disclosure may not apply in the same way. **Whether NRS 624.600 applies to a standard Las Vegas production tract purchase: NOT FOUND.** Do not assert it in reader-facing prose. NRS 624.602, by contrast, is written around a "purchaser of the residence" and clearly reaches new home sales.

### 2.3 The rest of the NRS 624.606 to 624.630 range

These sections govern payment, work stoppage and liability between owners, prime contractors and subcontractors, not builder-to-homebuyer disclosures. Headings verified [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-624.html | verified: 2026-07-25]:

- NRS 624.606 to 624.6086: definitions (higher-tiered contractor, lower-tiered subcontractor, owner, prime contractor).
- NRS 624.609 and 624.610: payment of the prime contractor during performance, grounds and procedure for withholding, stopping work or terminating.
- NRS 624.620: payment after the work is available for use or occupancy, withholding, notices of correction.
- NRS 624.622: notice requirements, prohibited provisions, exemptions, requests for information.
- NRS 624.624 to 624.628: lower-tiered subcontractor payment provisions.
- NRS 624.630: accrual and rate of interest on money due.

**Guide guidance:** do not use the 624.606 to 624.630 range for buyer content. It is contractor-to-contractor payment law and will confuse readers. Use 624.602 and the Recovery Fund instead.

### 2.4 The Residential Recovery Fund

The State Contractors Board collects a biennial assessment from residential contractors and may refer to the resulting account as the **Recovery Fund**. Assessment caps are $200 per biennium if the license monetary limit is not more than $1,000,000, $500 if more than $1,000,000 but limited, and $1,000 if unlimited [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-624.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 624.470).

An injured person who wants to recover from the account must file a complaint with the Board or its designee **within 4 years after the completion of qualified services** (NRS 624.480). Alternatively, within **2 years** after obtaining a judgment against a residential contractor, the injured person may apply to the Board for satisfaction of the judgment from the account (NRS 624.490). The Board must act on a complaint within **6 months** after it is filed and must give at least **30 days** notice of the hearing (NRS 624.500). Eligibility rules and recovery caps are in NRS 624.510.

**Maximum individual recovery amount and per-contractor aggregate cap from the Recovery Fund: NOT FOUND** (NRS 624.510 sets them but the dollar figures were not extracted in this pass). Do not state a dollar amount in the guide without pulling NRS 624.510 directly.

Substandard workmanship is separately a cause for discipline: workmanship not commensurate with standards of the trade in general, or below the building or construction codes adopted by the city or county where the work is performed, is cause for disciplinary action under NRS 624.300 [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-624.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 624.3017(1)).

State Contractors Board: https://www.nvcontractorsboard.com/ [verified: 2026-07-25].

## 3. The 1-2-10 warranty structure

### 3.1 What "1-2-10" means

"1-2-10" is shorthand for a three-tier new home warranty:

- **1 year, workmanship and materials.** The finish work and installed items: flooring, cabinets, doors, trim, paint, drywall, hardware.
- **2 years, systems (also called distribution systems).** Plumbing, electrical and HVAC distribution.
- **10 years, structural.** Qualifying structural defects in load-bearing elements such as the foundation and framing, typically backed by third-party insurance.

[source: https://www.strucsure.com/builders/our-builder-warranties/1-2-10-warranty/ | verified: 2026-07-25] and [source: https://www.2-10.com/builders-warranty/builder-faqs/ | verified: 2026-07-25]

### 3.2 Is 1-2-10 required by Nevada law? The honest answer.

**No, not as a three-tier package. Parts of it line up with Nevada law by coincidence of timing, not by mandate.**

- **The "1" is close to a legal floor.** Nevada does require a written builder's warranty on a new single-family residence, valid for **at least 1 year from completion of the written punch list**, covering home systems, workmanship, materials, plumbing, electrical and mechanical systems, appliances installed by contractors, fixtures, equipment and structural components (NRS 624.602) [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-624.html | verified: 2026-07-25]. Note that the statutory one-year minimum is actually **broader** than the typical private "1" tier, because NRS 624.602 requires the one-year warranty to reach systems and structural components too, unless a manufacturer or installer provides a separate warranty for them.
- **The "2" is not set by Nevada statute.** **No Nevada statute requiring a 2-year systems warranty: NOT FOUND.** The two-year systems tier is an industry convention carried in private warranty products.
- **The "10" is not a warranty requirement; it mirrors the statute of repose.** Nevada's 10-year outer limit comes from NRS 11.202, which caps how long **any** construction defect action may be brought after substantial completion. A 10-year structural warranty product roughly tracks that outer limit, but NRS 11.202 is a deadline to sue, not a promise to repair [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-011.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

Industry sources themselves describe the structure as "an industry standard, not a legal requirement everywhere" [source: https://www.costtobuildhouse.com/new-home-builder-warranty | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Safe reader-facing sentence:** "Nevada law requires your builder to give you a written warranty that lasts at least one year. The familiar 1-2-10 structure goes further than that, but the 2-year and 10-year pieces come from the builder's warranty company, not from Nevada law. Read the actual warranty book."

### 3.3 Why the 11-month walkthrough exists

Three separate deadlines converge at the end of year one, and this is the strongest, most defensible reason in the guide to schedule an 11-month inspection:

1. **The workmanship year is expiring.** Whether the builder's warranty is a private 1-2-10 or the statutory minimum under NRS 624.602, the broadest coverage tier ends around the one-year mark. NRS 624.602 measures that year from **completion of the written punch list**, so the true expiration date can differ from the closing anniversary. Readers should find the punch list completion date in their file.
2. **NRS 40.672 puts the builder on a 45-day repair clock only within the first year.** Written notice of a constructional defect given **not more than 1 year after the close of escrow of the initial purchase** obligates the builder to repair **within 45 days**, with State Contractors Board discipline under NRS 624.300 for failure to comply. After that first year, the homeowner drops into the ordinary Chapter 40 timeline: 90 days for the builder's written response, then 105 or 150 days to repair [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25].
3. **NRS 40.650(3) requires diligent pursuit of the builder's warranty** on a residence covered by one, and sums paid under a builder's warranty are deducted from any later recovery under NRS 40.650(1) [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25]. Letting the warranty lapse unused is not a neutral choice.

**Do an 11-month walkthrough, not a 12-month one, and put every item in writing.** Written notice is what triggers NRS 40.672. A verbal complaint to a warranty coordinator does not.

## 4. Builder purchase agreements: what buyers sign without reading

Builder contracts are the builder's own forms, drafted by the builder's counsel. They are not the standard resale purchase agreement Las Vegas buyers may have seen before. Everything in this section should be presented as "here is what these contracts commonly contain and what to look for," never as a claim about a specific builder's current form.

### 4.1 Binding arbitration and class action waivers

**What Nevada law says on its face.** NRS 597.995 provides that an agreement which includes a provision requiring a person to submit disputes to arbitration "must include specific authorization for the provision which indicates that the person has affirmatively agreed to the provision," and that if it does not, "the provision is void and unenforceable." Exceptions: collective bargaining agreements and certain will or trust arbitration provisions [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-597.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

**But that statute has been held preempted.** In *MMAWC, LLC v. Zion Wood Obi Wan Trust*, 448 P.3d 568 (Nev. 2019), decided September 5, 2019, the Nevada Supreme Court held that the Federal Arbitration Act **preempts NRS 597.995**, so the statute does not void an arbitration clause. The reasoning was that a state law which singles out and disfavors arbitration by imposing stricter requirements on arbitration provisions than on other contract provisions is preempted by the FAA [source: https://law.justia.com/cases/nevada/supreme-court/2019/75596.html | verified: 2026-07-25] and [source: https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=4930663900268165287 | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Accurate reader-facing framing (this one is easy to get wrong):** "You may see a separate line to initial next to the arbitration section. Nevada has a statute about that, but in 2019 the Nevada Supreme Court ruled that federal arbitration law overrides it. In plain terms: assume an arbitration clause in your builder contract is enforceable. If you sign it, you are most likely giving up your right to a jury trial and, in many contracts, your right to join a class action. Ask a Nevada attorney before you sign if this matters to you."

**Do not write** that Nevada law voids an unsigned arbitration clause. That was true on the face of NRS 597.995 and is no longer reliable after *MMAWC*.

**What arbitration does not erase.** Chapter 40's notice, inspection, right to repair, response and mediation steps are set by NRS 40.600 to 40.695, which "prevail over any conflicting law otherwise applicable to the claim" (NRS 40.635(2)) [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-040.html | verified: 2026-07-25]. **Whether and how a builder arbitration clause interacts with the Chapter 40 prelitigation process in a specific contract: NOT FOUND.** This is a genuine legal question and belongs to an attorney, not to this guide.

**Whether class action waivers specifically appear in Las Vegas builders' current purchase agreements: NOT FOUND.** No current Nevada builder purchase agreement was obtained in this pass. Frame class action waivers as "commonly paired with arbitration clauses in builder contracts nationally" and tell the reader to look for the term in their own contract.

### 4.2 The builder's right to change plans, materials and specifications

This one is verifiable from a builder's own published legal terms. Lennar's published legal disclaimers state, under "Substitutions": "The specific features in a home may vary from home to home and from one community to another. We reserve the right to substitute equipment, materials, appliances and brand names with items that have, in our sole opinion, equal or higher value. Color and size variations will occur." [source: https://www.lennar.com/legal | verified: 2026-07-25]

The same page also disclaims accuracy of floor plans, elevations, square footage, site plans, community maps, amenities and schools, and states that "Existing and proposed amenities for the communities are subject to changes, substitutions, and/or deletion without notice" and that Lennar "makes no representation or guarantees that the communities or any amenities will be built out as currently planned" [source: https://www.lennar.com/legal | verified: 2026-07-25]. The page self-identifies as "Website Legal Disclaimers (As of May 7, 2024)."

**Buyer-facing points:**
- "Equal or better, in the builder's sole opinion" is the operative phrase. The builder, not the buyer, decides whether a substitute is equivalent.
- Amenities shown on a community map are not promises. The pool, park or trail in the rendering can be changed or deleted.
- Renderings, model home finishes and marketing square footage are illustrations. What binds is the purchase agreement, the plan set and the options addendum.
- **Action item:** ask for the substitution clause in writing and ask whether the contract requires notice to the buyer before a material substitution, and whether the buyer has any right to object. **Whether Nevada law requires builder notice before substitution: NOT FOUND.** No such statute was located.

### 4.3 Escalation, cost-of-materials and price-change clauses

Lennar's published pricing disclaimer states: "All prices are subject to change without notice. Prices do not include closing costs and other fees to be paid by the buyer (including any builder fee described in the purchase agreement)." [source: https://www.lennar.com/legal | verified: 2026-07-25]

That disclaimer governs advertised prices on the website, not necessarily a signed contract price. **Whether Las Vegas builders' current purchase agreements contain post-signing price escalation or cost-of-materials clauses, and on what terms: NOT FOUND.** No executed or blank Nevada builder purchase agreement was obtained.

**Safe framing:** "Advertised prices change without notice until you sign. After you sign, whether your price can move depends entirely on your contract. Look for words like 'escalation,' 'cost of materials,' 'price adjustment,' or 'increase in the cost of labor or materials.' Ask the sales representative to point to the exact paragraph that locks your price, and get the answer in writing." Do not assert that escalation clauses are or are not common in Las Vegas without a source.

Also flag the phrase "any builder fee described in the purchase agreement." Builder fees are separate from closing costs, and buyers should ask what they are and how much.

### 4.4 Delay clauses and late delivery

Lennar's published "Completion Date" disclaimer states: "Unless otherwise noted in your purchase agreement, Lennar is required to complete, and does agree to complete, the construction of your home within a period of two (2) years from the date you sign your purchase agreement. If construction is delayed by any event recognized by the law of the state where your home is located as a defense to a contract action for non-performance or delay in performance, then the date of completion shall be extended by the delay period." The clause exists to keep the sale exempt from registration under the federal Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act [source: https://www.lennar.com/legal | verified: 2026-07-25].

**This is the single most useful and least understood fact in the whole contract section.** A two-year outside completion date is not a promise to deliver in eight months. The verbal estimate at the sales desk and the contractual deadline are different things, and only one is enforceable.

**Whether Nevada law entitles a buyer to money damages, rent reimbursement, or rate-lock extension costs when a builder delivers late: NOT FOUND.** No Nevada statute providing a delay remedy to new home buyers was located. Remedies depend on the contract, and builder contracts commonly extend the completion date for force majeure and similar events.

**Safe framing:** "Ask two questions before signing. First: what is the outside completion date in this contract, in writing? Second: what do I get if you miss it? For most builder contracts the honest answer to the second question is 'nothing,' and it is better to know that before your lease is up and your rate lock is expiring."

### 4.5 Is the contract negotiable at all?

**Be honest: the base contract is largely non-negotiable.** Production builders use a single form across a community and often across a division. A builder that changes contract terms for one buyer creates precedent for every other buyer in the same community, and it can complicate the lender, title and warranty relationships behind the sale. Sales representatives generally have no authority to redline the agreement.

**Note on sourcing:** the statement above is standard industry practice, not a cited legal fact. **A primary or authoritative source stating that Las Vegas builder purchase agreements are non-negotiable: NOT FOUND.** Present it in the guide as an experience-based observation from Ryan, not as law.

**What IS typically negotiable, and where a buyer's leverage actually lives:**

1. **Incentive dollars, not price.** Builders protect the recorded sale price because it sets the comp for every remaining home in the community. They will often move on incentives instead. Ask what the incentive is worth in dollars.
2. **Closing cost credits, usually tied to using the builder's affiliated lender.** Ask what the credit is if you use an outside lender, and compare the total cost, not just the credit.
3. **Rate buydowns and financing concessions** through the affiliated lender.
4. **Design center allowance or included options.** Sometimes easier to get than a price reduction.
5. **Structural options and lot premium** on a home not yet started.
6. **Which lot.** On a phase release, lot selection is real value: corner, cul-de-sac, orientation, backing to open space instead of a wall.
7. **Timing.** End of month, end of quarter and end of the builder's fiscal year change what a sales manager can approve. So does a standing inventory home that has been finished and unsold.
8. **Inventory or "quick move-in" homes** carry the most flexibility because the builder is carrying cost on a finished asset.

**Do not promise specific incentive amounts, buydown rates, or credit dollars in the guide. Those are community-specific and change monthly. Current Las Vegas builder incentive amounts: NOT FOUND in this pass** (that belongs to the builder-universe research file, not this one).

## 5. Earnest money and deposits in Nevada new construction

### 5.1 What Nevada law does and does not set

**There is no Nevada statute setting the amount of earnest money in a new construction purchase, and none making it refundable or non-refundable. Statutory earnest money amount or refundability rule for builder contracts: NOT FOUND.** The amount, the schedule and the forfeiture terms are set entirely by the builder's purchase agreement.

### 5.2 The one real statutory escape hatch: the 5-day cancellation right

Most Las Vegas new construction sits in a common-interest community (an HOA), which brings NRS Chapter 116 into play. This is a genuine, citable Nevada consumer protection and it belongs in the guide.

"A person required to deliver a public offering statement pursuant to subsection 3 of NRS 116.4102 shall provide a purchaser with a copy of the current public offering statement not later than the date on which an offer to purchase becomes binding on the purchaser. **Unless the purchaser has personally inspected the unit, the purchaser may cancel, by written notice, the contract of purchase until midnight of the fifth calendar day following the date of execution of the contract**, and the contract for purchase must contain a provision to that effect." [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-116.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 116.4108(1))

Cancellation is done by hand delivering notice to the offeror, or by mailing notice by prepaid United States mail to the offeror or the offeror's agent for service of process. "Cancellation is without penalty, and **all payments made by the purchaser before cancellation must be refunded promptly**." (NRS 116.4108(2))

The statutory information statement that must go to buyers in a common-interest community opens with: "YOU GENERALLY HAVE 5 DAYS TO CANCEL THE PURCHASE AGREEMENT?" and explains that the 5-day period starts on different dates depending on whether the buyer received a public offering statement (original purchaser) or a resale package [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-116.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 116.41095).

**Two accuracy warnings that must survive into reader-facing prose:**
1. The right in NRS 116.4108(1) is conditioned: "**Unless the purchaser has personally inspected the unit.**" A buyer who has walked the actual home may not have the 5-day right. Do not tell readers they always have five days.
2. It applies to purchases in a common-interest community where a public offering statement is required. Not every Las Vegas new build is in one. **Share of Clark County new construction that sits in a common-interest community: NOT FOUND.** Say "most new Las Vegas communities have an HOA" only if the builder-universe research file supports it; otherwise say "if your community has an HOA."

### 5.3 The other thing new construction buyers do not get

NRS 113.130 requires a seller of residential property to complete and serve the Seller's Real Property Disclosure form at least 10 days before conveyance, but subsection 2(c) exempts "the first sale of a residence that was constructed by a licensed contractor" [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-113.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Plain language for the guide:** "When you buy a resale home in Las Vegas, the seller has to fill out a disclosure form listing known defects. When you buy a brand new home from a builder, Nevada law does not require that form. Your protection is the inspection, the punch list, the written warranty and Chapter 40, not a disclosure sheet."

### 5.4 Typical deposit amounts

Reported ranges from Las Vegas agent blogs, **not primary sources and not verified against any builder contract**: earnest money roughly $5,000 to $15,000 at the pre-contract phase, and design center deposits roughly $2,500 to $8,500 [source: https://www.nevadarealestategroup.com/blog/new-construction-timeline-las-vegas-build-reality-2026/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Recommendation: do not print these numbers in the guide.** They come from a competing brokerage's blog with no underlying documentation, and per the no-fabrication rule a competitor's unsourced range is not good enough for a number a buyer will rely on. Either replace with figures Ryan can verify from actual Las Vegas builder contracts he has handled, or write the section without a dollar range: "Builders set their own deposit amounts, and they are usually larger than on a resale. Ask for the number and the refund terms in writing before you sign."

### 5.5 When deposits stop being refundable

The general pattern in builder contracts: earnest money is at greatest risk once the buyer moves past any contractual contingency period, and **design center and option deposits are commonly non-refundable as soon as the builder orders custom materials**, because those selections cannot be resold with the home. **Confirmation of this pattern from a Nevada builder contract or a primary source: NOT FOUND.**

**Safe framing for the guide, phrased as questions the buyer should ask before signing:**
- How much is the earnest money, and when is it due?
- Is there any period during which I can cancel and get it back? If so, how many days, and does it start at signing or at some other event?
- How much is the design center deposit, when is it due, and at what exact point does it become non-refundable?
- If my loan is denied, do I get my money back? Get the answer by paragraph number.
- If the builder misses the completion date, can I cancel and get my deposit back?

## 6. Agent representation at the model home

**This is the guide's primary call to action, so accuracy matters more here than anywhere else. Understate rather than overstate.**

### 6.1 The core fact: register your agent at the first contact, not the first signature

Builders set their own broker registration and cooperation policies. **The policies are not uniform and they are not law.** They are private business rules, and each builder can change its own.

**Lennar** publishes its Broker Participation Policy in its legal disclaimers. Verbatim, in relevant part:

> "While customers are free to use their own broker/agent when purchasing a home from Lennar, Lennar does not pay commissions to cooperating real estate brokerages in all communities. In order for a participating cooperating real estate brokerage ('Cooperating Broker') to receive a commission in connection with the sale of real property in a certain community, Lennar must be offering a commission in the community, and the Cooperating Broker must be documented on the first customer interaction with a Lennar employee. This means that the prospective buyer (the 'Prospect') must identify and register the Cooperating Broker: (i) when Prospect first contacts a Lennar employee about a home or community; (ii) when Prospect first discusses or is introduced to a community or home by Lennar's internet sales employees; (iii) when Prospect first visits a community; or (iv) when Prospect first attends a self-guided or virtual tour of a community presented by a Lennar Associate ..., whichever is first to occur. A failure of a Prospect to register Cooperating Broker upon the initial communication with Lennar about any community will render Cooperating Broker ineligible for commission. Registration alone of a Prospect by a Cooperating Broker is not sufficient for Cooperating Broker to be eligible for a commission. Cooperating Broker, or its affiliated sales associate, must also accompany the Prospect during Prospect's initial visit or initial self-guided tour of a home in a community. If Prospect is not local and does not visit the community in person, the Cooperating Broker, or its affiliated sales associate, must accompany Prospect on the first virtual tour."

The policy adds that registration is effective for **60 days** unless Lennar agrees otherwise in writing, extendable by another 60 days, and that a prospect who previously inquired without registering, or who registered at a sales office or took a self-guided tour without the broker present, makes the broker ineligible for a commission "in connection with the sale of real property in any Lennar community to such Prospect." [source: https://www.lennar.com/legal | verified: 2026-07-25] The page self-identifies as "Website Legal Disclaimers (As of May 7, 2024)."

Lennar separately states: "Booking an appointment on this website does not constitute a realtor registration as provided in the Lennar Broker Participation Policy." [source: https://www.lennar.com/legal | verified: 2026-07-25] That is a concrete trap worth naming in the guide.

**Richmond American Homes** publishes a co-op broker policy with materially different mechanics: the broker/agent must register the purchaser in writing at a community sales center, in writing at a Home Gallery location, or through the RichmondAmerican.com website, providing the purchaser's full name and either phone number or email. All registrations require confirmation from the purchaser within **four calendar days**. The broker relationship is recognized for **30 days** from the date the registration was submitted, after which the broker must re-register. Registrations are invalid for purchasers who registered at a Richmond American community during the 30 days prior to being validly registered. The commission percentage is set in the purchase agreement or in a written broker cooperation document signed by the purchaser and Richmond American's authorized representative [source: https://www.richmondamerican.com/broker-co-op-policy | verified: 2026-07-25].

**The contrast is the point.** Lennar requires the agent to physically accompany the buyer on the first visit. Richmond American's published policy does not contain an accompaniment requirement but does impose a 4-day purchaser confirmation and a 30-day registration life. Two large builders, two different rule sets.

**Correct reader-facing framing:**

> "Every builder has its own rule about when your agent has to be registered. Most want it at your very first contact, and some require your agent to walk in with you the first time. Some builders count a website appointment or an online inquiry as your first contact, so registering online without naming your agent can cost you representation before you ever set foot in a model home. The rules vary by builder and they change. Before you visit anything, call your agent, and let your agent confirm that community's registration rule."

**Do not write** "you must bring your agent on your first visit or you permanently lose representation." That overstates it. What a buyer can lose is the **builder's willingness to pay** that agent, and the specific rule differs by builder. A buyer is always free to hire and pay their own representation.

### 6.2 Who the model home sales representative works for

The person at the sales desk is the **builder's** employee or the builder's agent. Nevada's disclosure framework makes the point directly:

- A licensee acting as an agent in a real estate transaction must disclose to each party, as soon as is practicable, each source from which the licensee will receive compensation as a result of the transaction, and must provide the Real Estate Division's duties form to each party for whom the licensee is acting and to each unrepresented party [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-645.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 645.252(1)(b) and (3)).
- The Division is required to prepare and distribute those forms (NRS 645.193). The current form is "Duties Owed By A Nevada Real Estate Licensee," Form 525 [source: https://red.nv.gov/uploadedfiles/rednvgov/Content/Forms/525.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25].
- A licensee who has entered into a brokerage agreement to represent a client owes additional duties: reasonable skill and care to carry out the agreement, confidentiality for 1 year after termination, seeking terms acceptable to the client, presenting all offers, disclosing known material facts, advising the client to get expert advice beyond the licensee's expertise, and accounting for money and property (NRS 645.254). These duties **cannot be waived** (NRS 645.255) [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-645.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Plain language:** "The person in the model home is friendly, knowledgeable and paid by the builder. That is not a criticism, it is a job description. They owe the builder their loyalty. If nobody is representing you, nobody in that room is required to put your interests first."

### 6.3 Compensation: standard, but not guaranteed

**Say this carefully.** Builder-paid cooperating broker compensation is common, and where it applies the buyer's representation typically costs the buyer nothing out of pocket. **It is not universal.** Lennar states plainly that it "does not pay commissions to cooperating real estate brokerages in all communities," and that a commission requires both that Lennar is offering one in that community and that the broker was properly documented and accompanied the buyer [source: https://www.lennar.com/legal | verified: 2026-07-25].

Separately, since **August 17, 2024**, MLS participants working with buyers are required to enter into written agreements with buyers before touring a home, and those agreements must include a specific and conspicuous disclosure of the amount or rate of compensation the agent will receive or how it will be determined [source: https://www.nar.realtor/the-facts/what-the-nar-settlement-means-for-home-buyers-and-sellers | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Correct, defensible sentence for the guide:**

> "In most Las Vegas new home communities the builder pays the buyer's agent, so having representation usually costs you nothing extra. Builders do not offer it in every community, and the rules for earning it are strict. Since August 2024, you and your agent will sign a written agreement up front that spells out how your agent is paid. Ask about it before you tour, not after."

**Do not write** "representation is always free" or "the builder always pays your agent." Both are false.

### 6.4 A note on the "walk in without your agent and you lose everything" claim

Several Las Vegas agent blogs make strong versions of this claim, including advice to give a fake name when registering on a builder website [source: https://www.nevadarealestategroup.com/blog/do-you-need-realtor-new-construction-las-vegas-2026/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. **Do not repeat the fake-name advice.** It is bad practice, it is not something Ryan should put his license number next to, and it is unnecessary. The accurate and equally persuasive version is: register your agent at first contact, and let your agent make the first call.

Also, one such blog asserts "Nevada courts ruled that all sales agents and subcontractors work for the builder, not the home buyer." **No such Nevada case was located. Case citation: NOT FOUND.** Do not repeat that claim. The NRS 645.252 compensation-source disclosure and the Duties Owed form make the same point with a real citation.

## 7. NRS Chapter 645 advertising: why "Real Broker, LLC" appears on the guide

In any advertisement through which a licensee offers to perform services requiring a real estate license, the licensee must include his or her license number and, if a broker-salesperson or salesperson, must disclose the name of the brokerage with whom the licensee is associated. A broker-salesperson or salesperson may not advertise solely under his or her own name when acting in that capacity, and all such advertising must be done under the direct supervision of and in the name of the associated brokerage [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-645.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 645.315(1) and (2)).

**Practical requirement for the finished guide:** the guide is advertising by a licensee. It must carry Ryan Rose's Nevada license number and the brokerage name, Real Broker, LLC, and the presentation must be in the name of the brokerage rather than the individual alone. **Ryan's Nevada real estate license number: NOT FOUND in this research pass.** It must be supplied before publication.

The Real Estate Commission is authorized to adopt regulations on advertising under a nickname (NRS 645.315(3)). **Applicable NAC 645 advertising regulations: NOT FOUND** (not retrieved in this pass). If the guide uses any nickname, team name or DBA, check NAC 645 before publishing.

## 8. Inspection rights on a new build

### 8.1 Does a Nevada buyer have a legal right to bring an independent inspector?

**No Nevada statute granting a new home buyer the right to have an independent inspector on the builder's job site was located. Statutory inspection right: NOT FOUND.** Access to an active construction site is a contract and property-access question, so it is governed by the builder's purchase agreement and the builder's site rules.

What Nevada does regulate is **who may inspect**. Under NRS Chapter 645D, a person who prepares or communicates an inspection report must generally hold a certificate or license from the Real Estate Division. Each applicant and renewal applicant must show that the applicant or the applicant's employer carries errors-and-omissions coverage of **not less than $100,000** and general liability coverage of **not less than $100,000**, and must maintain that coverage. The Division adopts regulations prescribing education and experience requirements and a standard of practice and code of ethics establishing the degree of care a reasonably prudent certified inspector must exercise [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-645D.html | verified: 2026-07-25] (NRS 645D.120, 645D.190, 645D.100).

**Useful buyer-facing point:** "Ask to see your inspector's Nevada certificate. Nevada certifies home inspectors and requires them to carry insurance. Hire a certified one."

### 8.2 The four checkpoints

| Checkpoint | Timing | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-drywall (frame) inspection** | After framing, rough plumbing, rough electrical and HVAC rough-in, before insulation and drywall | The only time anyone can see the bones: framing, straps and hangers, plumbing and electrical runs, duct routing, window and door flashing, waterproofing. Once drywall goes on, none of it is visible again. |
| **Blue tape walkthrough (orientation)** | Days before closing | Cosmetic and finish issues get marked with blue tape and written into a punch list. **Insist the punch list is written**, because NRS 624.602 measures the statutory 1-year warranty from "the date of completion of a written punch list" [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-624.html \| verified: 2026-07-25]. |
| **Final walkthrough** | Immediately before closing | Confirm punch list items were actually completed, appliances present and working, systems operating. |
| **11-month warranty walkthrough** | About 11 months after closing | See Section 3.3. Catches items before the workmanship year and the NRS 40.672 45-day repair window close. |

### 8.3 Builder pushback a buyer should expect

Common builder objections to third-party inspections, reported by inspection-industry sources [source: https://greatinspector.com/home-inspections/the-inspection/new-construction/inspection-not-permitted/ | verified: 2026-07-25] and [source: https://www.texasinspector.com/2024/11/your-right-to-independent-inspections-during-construction/ | verified: 2026-07-25]:

- **"Our insurance does not allow non-employees on an active site."** Some builders require the inspector's certificate of insurance naming the builder as additional insured, with a waiver of subrogation and general liability coverage of at least $1,000,000 per occurrence.
- **"The city already inspects it."** Municipal inspection checks code minimums for the jurisdiction. It is not a buyer-side quality inspection and the inspector does not work for the buyer.
- **"We provide our own third-party inspection."** An inspector retained by the builder reports to the builder, and the buyer may not receive a written report.
- **Some builder contracts limit or disallow independent inspections outright**, which is precisely why this needs to be settled before signing.

**Note on sourcing:** these are inspection-industry sources describing national practice, not Nevada-specific or Clark County-specific. **Documented pushback by named Las Vegas builders: NOT FOUND.** Present as "here is what buyers commonly run into," not as a claim about any Las Vegas builder.

**Action items for the guide:**
1. Ask, **before signing**, whether independent inspections are permitted, at which stages, and what the inspector must provide.
2. Get the answer in the contract or in a written addendum, not verbally at the sales desk.
3. Schedule the pre-drywall inspection early. The window is short and the framing stage moves fast.
4. Put every walkthrough item in writing and keep a copy.

## 10. Claims the guide must NOT make

1. "Nevada's construction defect statute of repose is 6 years." It is **10 years** (NRS 11.202). The 6-year period existed only between February 24, 2015 and September 30, 2019.
2. "Nevada law voids an arbitration clause you did not separately initial." NRS 597.995 says so, but the Nevada Supreme Court held it preempted by the FAA in *MMAWC* (2019).
3. "Nevada law requires a 1-2-10 warranty." Nevada requires a written warranty of **at least 1 year** from completion of the written punch list (NRS 624.602). The 2 and the 10 are private warranty product tiers.
4. "You always have 5 days to cancel." NRS 116.4108(1) conditions the right on the purchaser **not** having personally inspected the unit, and applies to common-interest community purchases requiring a public offering statement.
5. "The builder always pays your agent, so representation is always free." Lennar's own policy says it does not pay cooperating brokers in all communities.
6. "Walk in without your agent and you permanently lose representation." What can be lost is the **builder-paid compensation**, and the rule differs by builder.
7. "All builders require your agent on the first visit." Lennar requires accompaniment; Richmond American's published policy does not.
8. Any specific dollar figure for earnest money, design center deposits, incentives or Recovery Fund caps, unless sourced before publication.
9. Any suggestion to give a false name when registering with a builder.

- Nevada Revised Statutes apply statewide, so NRS citations are not Clark County specific by nature. Clark County applicability is noted where relevant (for example, NRS 624.3017(1) measures workmanship against the building or construction codes adopted by the city or county where the work is performed, which for this guide means the City of Las Vegas, City of North Las Vegas, City of Henderson or unincorporated Clark County).

## 13. Required disclaimer language for the finished guide

The guide must carry something equivalent to:

> This guide is general information about Nevada law and Las Vegas new home buying. It is not legal advice, and reading it does not create an attorney-client or agency relationship. Laws change and builder contracts differ. Before you sign anything, have a Nevada attorney review your purchase agreement. Ryan Rose is a licensed Nevada real estate salesperson with Real Broker, LLC, not an attorney.

Plus, per NRS 645.315: Ryan's Nevada license number and the brokerage name, Real Broker, LLC.
